name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_STATEMENT_Q01 - Isolated system definition and thermos flask example

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:

Statement I: In an isolated system, there is no exchange of either energy or matter between the system and the surroundings.

Statement II: Reactants placed in a thermos flask or any other closed insulated vessel form an example of an isolated system.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Thermodynamic systems are classified into open, closed, and isolated systems based on whether matter and energy can cross the boundary between the system and the surroundings.

Step 2: Evaluation
By definition, an isolated system permits neither energy nor matter to be exchanged with the surroundings. A closed, thermally insulated vessel such as a thermos flask prevents both heat/work transfer and matter transfer across its boundary, making it a valid example of an isolated system. Thus, both statements are correct.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both statements are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_STATEMENT_Q02 - State functions versus path functions q and w

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:

Statement I: Internal energy \(U\), pressure \(p\), volume \(V\), and temperature \(T\) are state functions because their values depend only on the state of the system and not on how it is reached.

Statement II: Heat \(q\) and work \(w\) are also state functions because \(q + w = \Delta U\) is independent of the path taken.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A state function depends solely on the initial and final equilibrium states of a system, whereas a path function depends on how the change is carried out.

Step 2: Evaluation
Quantities such as \(U\), \(p\), \(V\), and \(T\) are indeed state functions because their changes depend only on the initial and final states. However, for a given change in state, \(q\) and \(w\) individually vary depending on the path taken (for example, reversible versus irreversible expansion); only their sum \(q + w = \Delta U\) is independent of path. Therefore, the first claim is true, whereas the claim that \(q\) and \(w\) are state functions is false.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The first statement is correct, while the second statement is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_STATEMENT_Q03 - Heat at constant volume and constant pressure

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:

Statement I: For any process carried out at constant volume (\(\Delta V = 0\)), the enthalpy change \(\Delta H\) is always zero.

Statement II: The heat absorbed by a system at constant pressure, \(q_p\), equals the enthalpy change \(\Delta H\) and is independent of path.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
By definition, \(H = U + pV\), so \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta(pV)\). At constant volume (\(\Delta V = 0\)), \(\Delta U = q_v\), whereas at constant pressure, \(\Delta H = q_p\).

Step 2: Evaluation
At constant volume, \(\Delta U = q_v\) is not zero in general, and \(\Delta H = \Delta U + V\Delta p\) need not be zero; hence the claim that \(\Delta H\) is always zero at constant volume is false. On the other hand, at constant pressure, \(q_p = \Delta H\), and since enthalpy \(H\) is a state function, \(q_p\) is independent of path.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The first statement is incorrect, while the second statement is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_STATEMENT_Q04 - Definition of standard molar enthalpy of formation

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:

Statement I: The standard enthalpy change for the reaction \(\mathrm{H_2(g) + Br_2(l) \rightarrow 2HBr(g)}\) is equal to the standard molar enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^\ominus\)) of \(\mathrm{HBr(g)}\).

Statement II: The standard enthalpy change for the reaction \(\mathrm{CaO(s) + CO_2(g) \rightarrow CaCO_3(s)}\) is equal to the standard molar enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^\ominus\)) of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Standard molar enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^\ominus\)) is defined strictly as the enthalpy change when \(1\text{ mol}\) of a compound is formed from its constituent elements in their most stable reference states.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(\mathrm{H_2(g) + Br_2(l) \rightarrow 2HBr(g)}\), two moles of \(\mathrm{HBr(g)}\) are formed rather than one mole, so \(\Delta_r H^\ominus = 2\Delta_f H^\ominus(\mathrm{HBr, g})\). In \(\mathrm{CaO(s) + CO_2(g) \rightarrow CaCO_3(s)}\), \(\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)}\) is formed from other compounds rather than from its constituent elements. Thus, both statements are incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both statements are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_STATEMENT_Q05 - Extensive nature of enthalpy and reversing thermochemical equations

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:

Statement I: Enthalpy \(H\) is an extensive property, whereas molar enthalpy \(H_{\mathrm{m}}\) is an intensive property.

Statement II: When a balanced chemical equation is reversed, the numerical magnitude of \(\Delta_r H^\ominus\) remains unchanged while its sign is reversed.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Extensive properties depend on the amount of substance, whereas molar properties (obtained by dividing by \(n\)) are independent of sample size. Furthermore, because enthalpy is a state function, \(\Delta_r H^\ominus = H_{\text{products}} - H_{\text{reactants}}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Enthalpy scales with the number of moles (extensive), while molar enthalpy \(H_{\mathrm{m}} = H/n\) is for \(1\text{ mol}\) and is intensive. Reversing a reaction swaps reactants and products, which negates \(\Delta_r H^\ominus\) while preserving its magnitude. Thus, both statements are correct.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both statements are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_STATEMENT_Q06 - Bomb calorimetry and relation between delta H and delta U

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:

Statement I: In a bomb calorimeter, the reaction occurs in a sealed steel vessel at constant volume (\(\Delta V = 0\)), so no pressure-volume work is done and the heat measured equals \(\Delta U\).

Statement II: For every chemical reaction involving gases carried out in a bomb calorimeter, \(\Delta H\) is always strictly equal to \(\Delta U\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A bomb calorimeter is a rigid, sealed container (\(\Delta V = 0\)), so \(w = 0\) and \(\Delta U = q_v\). However, \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta U\) are related by \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The heat measured in a bomb calorimeter indeed equals \(\Delta U\) because \(\Delta V = 0\). However, for reactions involving gases where \(\Delta n_g \neq 0\), \(\Delta H\) differs from \(\Delta U\) by \(\Delta n_g RT\); they are equal only when \(\Delta n_g = 0\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The first statement is correct, while the second statement is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_STATEMENT_Q07 - Gibbs energy criterion and temperature effect on spontaneity

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:

Statement I: Every exothermic reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures, whereas every endothermic reaction is non-spontaneous at all temperatures.

Statement II: At constant temperature and pressure, a process is spontaneous if its Gibbs energy change \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) is negative (\(\Delta G < 0\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Spontaneity at constant \(T\) and \(p\) depends on both enthalpy and entropy changes through \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S < 0\).

Step 2: Evaluation
An exothermic reaction (\(\Delta H < 0\)) with \(\Delta S < 0\) becomes non-spontaneous at high temperatures when \(|T\Delta S| > |\Delta H|\). Conversely, an endothermic reaction (\(\Delta H > 0\)) with \(\Delta S > 0\) becomes spontaneous at high temperatures when \(T\Delta S > \Delta H\). Hence, the claim about all exothermic and endothermic reactions is false. Meanwhile, \(\Delta G < 0\) is indeed the exact criterion for spontaneity at constant \(T\) and \(p\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The first statement is incorrect, while the second statement is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_STATEMENT_Q08 - Standard Gibbs energy at equilibrium and third law scope

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct option:

Statement I: At dynamic equilibrium for a reversible chemical reaction, the standard Gibbs energy change \(\Delta_r G^\ominus\) is always equal to zero.

Statement II: According to the third law of thermodynamics, the entropy of any supercooled liquid or aqueous solution approaches zero as the temperature approaches \(0\text{ K}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
At chemical equilibrium, the reaction Gibbs energy \(\Delta_r G\) is zero, whereas \(\Delta_r G^\ominus = -RT\ln K\). The third law of thermodynamics applies strictly to pure crystalline solids.

Step 2: Evaluation
At equilibrium, \(\Delta_r G = 0\), not \(\Delta_r G^\ominus\) (which equals zero only when \(K = 1\)). Furthermore, theoretical and experimental evidence shows that solutions and supercooled liquids retain residual disorder and do not have zero entropy at \(0\text{ K}\); only pure crystalline substances approach zero entropy at \(0\text{ K}\). Thus, both statements are incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both statements are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
